subject: A
topic: Rapid mixed revision & weak-area drill — General English

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct option: ______ Andaman and Nicobar Islands form a Union Territory of India.
questions.explanation: Groups of islands take the definite article, as in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, the Maldives and the Lakshadweep. 'A' is wrong because the indefinite article cannot precede a plural proper noun. 'An' is wrong on the same ground and also because 'Andaman' would need a vowel sound only for the a/an choice, which does not arise for a plural name. 'No article' is wrong because although single islands drop the article (Sri Lanka, Java), archipelagos and island groups regularly keep 'the'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: The delegation finally prevailed __________ the minister to reconsider the transfer order. Fill in the blank with the correct preposition: __________
questions.explanation: 'Prevail upon' (or 'prevail on') means to persuade someone successfully, which is the sense required here. 'over' is wrong because 'prevail over' means to defeat or triumph over an opponent, as in 'justice prevailed over prejudice'. 'with' is wrong because 'prevail with' is not standard modern usage in the sense of persuading. 'against' is wrong because it reverses the meaning into resistance or opposition, which contradicts the minister actually agreeing to reconsider.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the idioms in Column I with their meanings in Column II:

Column I:
(a) To carry the day
(b) To cut the Gordian knot
(c) To have an axe to grind
(d) To draw a blank

Column II:
(i) To settle a difficulty by bold and decisive action
(ii) To have a private or selfish interest to serve
(iii) To fail to obtain any result
(iv) To win or be successful

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: 'Carry the day' means to win; 'cut the Gordian knot' recalls Alexander slicing the knot and means to solve a problem by bold action; 'have an axe to grind' means to have a selfish motive; 'draw a blank' means to get no result. The option swapping the first two is wrong because winning and bold problem-solving are distinct ideas. The option pairing the Gordian knot with a selfish motive is wrong because that phrase carries no suggestion of self-interest. The option pairing 'carry the day' with failure inverts its meaning entirely.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct option: Hardly ______ the whistle when the crowd surged forward.
questions.explanation: When a negative or restrictive adverb such as 'hardly', 'scarcely' or 'no sooner' begins a sentence, the auxiliary is inverted before the subject, giving 'Hardly had he blown'. 'he had blown' is wrong because it keeps normal word order and ignores the mandatory inversion. 'did he blew' is wrong because after the auxiliary 'did' the bare infinitive 'blow' is required, not the past form 'blew'. 'he has blown' is wrong both for lacking inversion and for using the present perfect with a past narrative.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following are grammatically correct sentences?

(i) The jury has given its verdict.
(ii) One of my friends is a police officer.
(iii) Neither of the two candidates were selected.
(iv) The number of applicants was very large.

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: (i) is correct because a collective noun acting as one body takes a singular verb and 'its'. (ii) is correct because the subject is 'one', not 'friends'. (iv) is correct because 'the number of' is singular, unlike 'a number of', which is plural. (iii) is WRONG because 'neither' is singular and requires 'was selected'. Hence every option containing (iii) must be rejected.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the word most nearly similar in meaning to 'PERFUNCTORY'.
questions.explanation: 'Perfunctory' describes something done merely as a formality, with little care or interest, so 'superficial' is the closest synonym. 'Thorough' is wrong because it means complete and careful in every detail, the direct opposite of a perfunctory effort. 'Punctual' is wrong because it concerns being on time and is a trap for candidates who link 'perfunctory' with 'punctual' by sound. 'Courteous' is wrong because it refers to politeness of manner, which says nothing about the carelessness with which a task is performed.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In the sentence 'Let you and me settle this quietly', the form 'me' is correct.
Reason (R): A pronoun that follows the verb 'let' stands as its object and therefore takes the objective case.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: (A) is correct because 'let' is followed by objects, so 'you and me' is right and 'you and I' is a common error. (R) is correct because it states exactly the rule of case governing objects of a verb. (R) therefore explains (A). The second option is wrong because the rule cited is precisely the reason for the form. The third option is wrong because the objective-case rule after 'let' is genuine. The fourth option is wrong because 'Let you and me' is the accepted construction.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the sentence in which the semicolon has been used correctly.
options: The inquiry was completed; because the evidence was clear.
The inquiry was completed; and the report was submitted the next day.
The inquiry was completed; the report was submitted the next day.
The inquiry; which took a week, was finally completed.
questions.correctAnswer: The inquiry was completed; the report was submitted the next day.
questions.explanation: A semicolon joins two closely related INDEPENDENT clauses without a conjunction, which is exactly what the correct sentence does. The version with 'and' after the semicolon is wrong because a coordinating conjunction makes the semicolon redundant; a comma should be used. The version with 'because' is wrong because what follows is a dependent clause, and a semicolon cannot precede a subordinate clause. The last version is wrong because it separates the subject from its verb, a place where no semicolon may stand.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about the use of tenses:

(i) The present perfect is not used along with a definite past adverbial such as 'yesterday'.
(ii) In reported speech a present tense normally shifts to the past when the reporting verb is in the past.
(iii) 'I am living here since 2019' is the correct form for an action continuing from a past point.
(iv) The simple present is used for timetables and scheduled future events.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement (i) is correct — we say 'He came yesterday', not 'He has come yesterday'. Statement (ii) is correct — that is the standard backshift rule of indirect speech. Statement (iv) is correct — 'The train leaves at six' describes a fixed schedule. Statement (iii) is FALSE because an action beginning in the past and still continuing requires the present perfect continuous: 'I have been living here since 2019'. Every option containing (iii) is therefore wrong.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the sentence in which the confusable word has been used correctly.
options: The counsel advised his client to remain silent.
The counsel adviced his client to remain silent.
The council advised its client to remain silent.
The counsel advise his client to remain silent.
questions.correctAnswer: The counsel advised his client to remain silent.
questions.explanation: 'Counsel' means a lawyer and 'advise' is the verb (with an s), so 'The counsel advised his client' is correct. 'adviced' is wrong because 'advice' is the noun and has no verb forms; the past tense must be 'advised'. The version with 'council' is wrong because a council is an administrative body and does not appear in court for a client. The last version is wrong because 'advise' is left in the base form where a past tense is needed for a completed act.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the pairs in Column I with the relationship in Column II:

Column I:
(a) Ornithologist : Birds
(b) Cardiologist : Heart
(c) Philatelist : Stamps
(d) Numismatist : Coins

Column II:
(i) Specialist in the diseases of this organ
(ii) Collector and student of these
(iii) Scientist who studies these creatures
(iv) Collector of these adhesive labels

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: An ornithologist studies birds, a cardiologist treats the heart, a philatelist collects postage stamps and a numismatist collects and studies coins. The option pairing the ornithologist with the heart specialist is wrong because ornithology is zoological, not medical. The option pairing the philatelist with coin collecting and the numismatist with stamps is wrong because it interchanges the two collectors. The option pairing the ornithologist with coin collecting misplaces a scientific discipline as a hobby.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct preposition: The two accounts of the incident are at variance ______ each other.
questions.explanation: The fixed phrase is 'at variance with', meaning in disagreement or conflict with. 'from' is wrong because 'from' follows expressions of difference such as 'different from' or 'derived from', not 'at variance'. 'to' is wrong because 'to' follows comparatives of rank such as 'superior to' and 'prior to'. 'against' is wrong because although it suggests opposition, the idiom does not admit it; 'at variance against' is not used in standard English.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following are correct prepositional collocations?

(i) Deprived of
(ii) Comply with
(iii) Superior than
(iv) Abide by

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: 'Deprived of', 'comply with' and 'abide by' are all established collocations, as in deprived of rights, comply with orders and abide by a decision. 'Superior than' is WRONG because Latin comparatives such as superior, inferior, senior, junior and prior are followed by 'to', giving 'superior to'. Hence every option containing (iii) must be rejected, and the option omitting 'abide by' leaves out a standard legal collocation.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the word most opposite in meaning to 'AMELIORATE'.
questions.explanation: 'Ameliorate' means to make a bad situation better, so its antonym is 'worsen'. 'Improve' is wrong because it is a synonym of ameliorate, not an antonym. 'Postpone' is wrong because it concerns delay in time rather than a change in quality or condition. 'Clarify' is wrong because it means to make something clear or intelligible, which relates to understanding rather than to improvement or deterioration of a state of affairs.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In the sentence 'The children go to school by bus', no article is used before 'school'.
Reason (R): In English the article is always omitted before the names of all buildings.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: (A) is correct but (R) is not correct
questions.explanation: (A) is correct because when an institution is referred to for its primary purpose — school for study, church for worship, hospital as a patient — the article is dropped. (R) is FALSE because the omission is not a rule about buildings at all: we say 'the post office', 'the library' and even 'the school' when the physical building is meant, as in 'the painters are at the school'. The first two options are wrong because they require (R) to be true, and the fourth is wrong because (A) is accurate.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: In the sentence 'That he was innocent became clear only later', the clause 'That he was innocent' functions as:
questions.explanation: The noun clause answers 'what became clear?' and so occupies the subject position before the verb 'became'. 'The object of the verb' is wrong because 'became' is a linking verb and takes a complement, not an object, and in any case the clause precedes it. 'The complement of an adjective' is wrong because the complement here is the adjective 'clear' itself, which follows the verb. 'An adverbial modifier' is wrong because the clause does not tell how, when, where or why; removing it would leave the sentence without a subject.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Neither the commandant nor his deputies __________ available at that hour. Fill in the blank with the correct verb form: __________
questions.explanation: With 'neither ... nor' the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it, and the nearer subject 'deputies' is plural, so 'were' is required. 'was' is wrong because it would agree with 'commandant', which is the FARTHER subject. 'is' is wrong because the sentence is set in past time by 'at that hour' in a narrative frame, and it is also singular. 'has been' is wrong because the present perfect clashes with the definite past reference and again fails the proximity rule of number.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about punctuation:

(i) A colon may be used to introduce a list or an explanation.
(ii) A semicolon can join two independent clauses without a conjunction.
(iii) An apostrophe is used to form the plural of ordinary nouns.
(iv) A hyphen joins the parts of a compound adjective placed before a noun.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement (i) is correct — 'He carried three items: a torch, a rope and a whistle.' Statement (ii) is correct — that is the primary function of the semicolon. Statement (iv) is correct — 'a well-known officer', 'a five-year term'. Statement (iii) is FALSE because ordinary plurals are formed with -s alone; the apostrophe marks possession or contraction, and writing 'photo's' for the plural is a standard error. Every option containing (iii) is therefore wrong.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: What does the idiom 'to throw down the gauntlet' mean?
questions.explanation: The phrase comes from the medieval practice of flinging down an armoured glove to challenge an opponent to combat, and it now means to issue a challenge openly. 'To surrender without a struggle' is wrong because that is the opposite; surrender would be signalled by 'throw in the towel'. 'To dismiss a serious accusation' is wrong because the idiom initiates a contest rather than brushing one aside. 'To postpone an awkward decision' is wrong because delay is conveyed by expressions such as 'kick the can down the road'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the words in Column I with their meanings in Column II:

Column I:
(a) Ephemeral
(b) Meticulous
(c) Garrulous
(d) Innocuous

Column II:
(i) Extremely careful about small details
(ii) Talking far too much
(iii) Harmless and unlikely to offend
(iv) Lasting for a very short time

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: 'Ephemeral' means short-lived, 'meticulous' means painstakingly careful, 'garrulous' means excessively talkative and 'innocuous' means harmless. The option pairing 'ephemeral' with carefulness is wrong because ephemerality concerns duration, not diligence. The option pairing 'meticulous' with talkativeness is wrong because meticulousness is about precision, not speech. The option pairing 'ephemeral' with harmlessness and 'innocuous' with brevity confuses the ideas of danger and duration.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: He is more taller than I.
He is taller than me am.
He is taller than I am.
questions.correctAnswer: He is taller than I am.
questions.explanation: When 'than' introduces a clause, the pronoun is the subject of that clause, so 'than I am' is correct. 'than me am' is wrong because the objective 'me' cannot be the subject of the verb 'am'. 'more taller' is wrong because 'taller' is already a comparative and cannot take 'more' as well, a double comparative. 'than myself' is wrong because a reflexive pronoun needs an antecedent in the same clause and cannot serve as the second term of a comparison.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following are correctly formed plural nouns?

(i) Criteria
(ii) Phenomenons
(iii) Mothers-in-law
(iv) Passers-by

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: 'Criteria' is the correct plural of 'criterion'; 'mothers-in-law' pluralises the principal word 'mother'; 'passers-by' likewise pluralises 'passer'. 'Phenomenons' is WRONG because the Greek-derived plural of 'phenomenon' is 'phenomena', exactly parallel to criterion and criteria. Hence every option containing (ii) must be rejected, and the option that drops 'criteria' discards a correctly formed classical plural.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Complete the analogy: Sculptor : Chisel :: Blacksmith : ?
questions.explanation: The relationship is craftsman to the characteristic implement of his craft; the blacksmith shapes heated metal on an anvil, just as a sculptor works with a chisel. 'Loom' is wrong because a loom belongs to a weaver. 'Scalpel' is wrong because a scalpel is the surgeon's instrument. 'Trowel' is wrong because a trowel is used by a mason or gardener; only the anvil completes the smith-and-forge association.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The standard formal expression is 'different than'.
Reason (R): Adjectives of comparison such as 'similar' and 'different' are followed by prepositions rather than by conjunctions.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: (A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.explanation: (A) is FALSE because standard formal usage is 'different from'; 'different than' is a colloquial American variant not accepted in careful writing. (R) is TRUE because 'similar to', 'different from' and 'identical with' all take prepositions, whereas 'than' is the conjunction used after comparatives such as 'taller'. The first two options are wrong because they require (A) to be correct, and the third is wrong because the prepositional rule stated in (R) is sound.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about clauses:

(i) A noun clause can act as the object of a preposition.
(ii) An adjective clause normally begins with a relative pronoun or a relative adverb.
(iii) An adverb clause of concession is introduced by conjunctions such as 'though' and 'although'.
(iv) A coordinate clause depends on another clause for its grammatical completeness.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement (i) is correct — in 'He is sure of what he saw', the noun clause follows the preposition 'of'. Statement (ii) is correct — who, whom, whose, which, that, where and when introduce adjective clauses. Statement (iii) is correct — though, although and even if express concession. Statement (iv) is FALSE because coordinate clauses are of EQUAL rank, joined by and, but or or, and each can stand alone; dependence is the mark of a subordinate clause.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct option: He was appointed ______ Deputy Superintendent of Police last year.
questions.explanation: After verbs such as appoint, elect, make and choose, a unique office or title is used without an article: 'He was appointed Deputy Superintendent of Police', 'She was elected Chairperson'. 'the' is wrong because the definite article would be needed only if the post were being identified among others, as in 'the Deputy Superintendent who signed the order'. 'a' is wrong because it would treat a titled office as one of many similar things. 'an' is wrong for that reason and also because 'Deputy' begins with a consonant sound.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: After the irregularities came to light, the officer had to __________ the music. Fill in the blank to complete the idiom: __________
questions.explanation: The idiom is 'to face the music', meaning to accept the unpleasant consequences of one's actions. 'hear' is wrong because 'hear the music' is a literal phrase with no idiomatic force of accountability. 'play' is wrong because 'play the music' again reads literally, and the related idiom 'call the tune' has an altogether different sense of being in control. 'take' is wrong because 'take the music' is not an English idiom at all; the fixed collocation admits only 'face'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct option: By next December, she ______ ten years of service in the force.
questions.explanation: 'By next December' fixes a point in the future before which the action will be finished, which is exactly the work of the future perfect, 'will have completed'. 'will complete' is wrong because the simple future states that the action happens at that time rather than being already complete by then. 'would complete' is wrong because 'would' expresses a conditional or a past-in-future, not a plain future fact. 'has completed' is wrong because the present perfect cannot reach forward to a future deadline.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the words in Column I with their antonyms in Column II:

Column I:
(a) Lucid
(b) Candid
(c) Frugal
(d) Docile

Column II:
(i) Extravagant
(ii) Obscure
(iii) Unruly
(iv) Evasive

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: 'Lucid' (clear) is opposed by 'obscure'; 'candid' (frank) by 'evasive'; 'frugal' (thrifty) by 'extravagant'; 'docile' (submissive) by 'unruly'. The option pairing 'lucid' with 'evasive' is wrong because evasiveness opposes frankness, not clarity of expression. The option pairing 'frugal' with 'unruly' is wrong because unruliness concerns discipline, not spending. The option pairing 'lucid' with 'unruly' and 'docile' with 'obscure' mismatches qualities of expression with qualities of temperament.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the word most nearly similar in meaning to 'INDIGENOUS'.
questions.explanation: 'Indigenous' means originating naturally in a particular place, so 'native' is the exact synonym, as in indigenous crafts or native species. 'Imported' is wrong because imported goods come from elsewhere, the opposite of indigenous. 'Primitive' is wrong because it suggests an early or undeveloped stage and carries a judgement about level of advancement, which 'indigenous' does not. 'Abundant' is wrong because it refers to quantity rather than to place of origin.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following are correct uses of the definite article?

(i) The Himalayas are the highest mountain system in the world.
(ii) The honesty is the best policy.
(iii) The rich should help the poor.
(iv) The Indian Ocean lies to the south of India.

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: (i) is correct because mountain ranges take 'the'. (iii) is correct because 'the' before an adjective forms a plural class noun, 'the rich' meaning rich people. (iv) is correct because oceans and seas take 'the'. (ii) is WRONG because abstract nouns used in a general sense take no article; the proverb is 'Honesty is the best policy'. Hence every option containing (ii) must be rejected.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The words 'complement' and 'compliment' cannot be used interchangeably.
Reason (R): The two words are pronounced almost identically in ordinary speech.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: (A) is correct because 'complement' means something that completes, while 'compliment' means an expression of praise. (R) is also correct, since the two are near-homophones. But (R) does not explain (A): the words must be kept apart because their MEANINGS and origins differ, and identical pronunciation is in fact the reason people confuse them rather than the reason they differ. The first option is wrong for that reason, and the third and fourth are wrong because both statements are true.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Which sentence uses commas correctly?
options: My colleague, who joined last year, has been promoted.
My colleague who joined last year, has been promoted.
My colleague, who joined last year has been promoted.
My colleague who, joined last year, has been promoted.
questions.correctAnswer: My colleague, who joined last year, has been promoted.
questions.explanation: A non-defining relative clause must be enclosed by a pair of commas, one before 'who' and one after 'year'. The second option is wrong because it opens the clause without a comma while closing it with one, leaving the pair unbalanced. The third option is wrong for the mirror-image fault of omitting the closing comma, which then wrongly separates nothing. The fourth option is wrong because it places a comma between the relative pronoun and its verb, which is never permitted.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about pronouns:

(i) In traditional usage 'each other' is used of two persons and 'one another' of more than two.
(ii) A relative pronoun agrees with its antecedent in number and person.
(iii) 'Whose' may be used only of persons and never of things.
(iv) An emphatic pronoun can be removed without making the sentence ungrammatical.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement (i) is correct as the traditional distinction. Statement (ii) is correct — 'It is I who am responsible' shows agreement in person. Statement (iv) is correct — in 'I myself saw it', dropping 'myself' leaves a complete sentence, unlike a reflexive object. Statement (iii) is FALSE because 'whose' is regularly used of things, as in 'a rule whose meaning is unclear'. Every option containing (iii) is therefore wrong.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the word most opposite in meaning to 'INTREPID'.
questions.explanation: 'Intrepid' means fearless and undaunted in the face of danger, so its antonym is 'timid', meaning easily frightened. 'Fearless' is wrong because it is a synonym of intrepid rather than its opposite. 'Reckless' is wrong because recklessness is courage without judgement and therefore lies on the same side of the scale as intrepidity, only in excess. 'Restless' is wrong because it describes an inability to stay still or be content, which has nothing to do with the presence or absence of fear.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct preposition: The officer was absolved ______ all blame after the departmental inquiry.
questions.explanation: 'Absolve somebody of' (or occasionally 'from') blame or responsibility is the accepted pattern, and 'absolved of all blame' is the standard collocation. 'from' is wrong in this fixed phrase because 'from' usually follows verbs of separation such as 'prohibit from' and 'refrain from'. 'for' is wrong because 'for' follows verbs of punishment or reward, as in 'punished for negligence'. 'against' is wrong because it expresses opposition and cannot follow 'absolve' at all.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: What does the idiom 'a storm in a teacup' mean?
options: Great excitement over a trifling matter
A sudden and violent family quarrel
An unexpected piece of good fortune
questions.correctAnswer: Great excitement over a trifling matter
questions.explanation: 'A storm in a teacup' describes a great deal of fuss and anger about something of very little importance. 'A sudden and violent family quarrel' is wrong because the idiom stresses the triviality of the cause rather than the domestic setting of the dispute. 'A well-concealed and serious danger' is wrong because that idea belongs to phrases such as 'a snake in the grass'. 'An unexpected piece of good fortune' is wrong because the expression carries no suggestion of luck or benefit.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about prepositions:

(i) 'Since' is used with a point of time and 'for' with a period of time.
(ii) 'Between' is used of two persons or things and 'among' of more than two.
(iii) 'In' is used before a specific date and 'on' before the name of a month.
(iv) 'By' indicates the latest time at which something will be done.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement (i) is correct — 'since Monday' but 'for three days'. Statement (ii) is correct as the traditional distinction of number. Statement (iv) is correct — 'submit it by Friday' fixes a deadline. Statement (iii) is FALSE because the usage is the reverse: 'on 15 August' for a specific date and 'in August' for a month or longer period. Every option containing (iii) is therefore wrong.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Identify the sentence that is free from any error of word choice.
options: The new rule will have no affect on the recruits.
The new rule will effect all recruits equally.
The new rule will affect all recruits equally.
The new rule will loose its force after a year.
questions.correctAnswer: The new rule will affect all recruits equally.
questions.explanation: 'Affect' is the verb meaning to influence, so 'will affect all recruits' is right. The version using 'effect' as the verb is wrong because 'effect' as a verb means to bring about or accomplish, as in 'effect a change', which cannot govern 'all recruits'. The version with 'no affect' is wrong because the NOUN form is 'effect'. The last version is wrong because 'loose' means slack or to release, whereas the verb required is 'lose'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: In the sentence 'He behaved as though nothing had happened', the subordinate clause is an:
questions.explanation: 'As though nothing had happened' tells HOW he behaved and is introduced by the conjunction 'as though', which marks manner or comparison. 'Adverb clause of reason' is wrong because a reason clause answers 'why' and begins with because, since or as. 'Adjective clause' is wrong because the group qualifies no noun or pronoun in the main clause. 'Noun clause' is wrong because it cannot be replaced by a noun functioning as subject or object; the sentence would collapse without a manner adverbial.
